title: Group Words by Length
oneLiner: Build a dictionary from each word length to the list of words with that length, keeping their original order.
keyTakeaway: Grouping is a dictionary of lists: for each item, find its key and append it to that key's list, creating the list the first time. LINQ does it with GroupBy(...).ToDictionary(...); Python with defaultdict(list) or setdefault.
explanation:
Write GroupByLength(words), returning a dictionary whose keys are word lengths and whose values are the words of that length, in the order they appeared. ["fan", "pump", "cat", "valve", "gear"] gives {3: ["fan", "cat"], 4: ["pump", "gear"], 5: ["valve"]}. Duplicates are kept, and an empty list gives an empty dictionary. (The tests show the keys as strings, "3", because that's how JSON writes dictionary keys; your dictionary uses ints.)

The loop version works in both languages: for each word, look up its length; if that key isn't in the dictionary yet, add an empty list; then append the word. Python's collections.defaultdict(list) creates the empty list for you, and dict.setdefault(key, []).append(word) does the same with a plain dict.

Then try the one-expression versions from the LINQ and Comprehensions lesson: words.GroupBy(w => w.Length) .ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.ToList()) in C#. GroupBy keeps the items in each group in their original order. Python has no single built-in that groups without sorting first (itertools.groupby only groups neighbours), so the loop with a defaultdict is the usual answer.

visualizationSteps.message: Start with an empty dictionary of lists.
"fan" has length 3, a new key: start an empty list and add it.
"pump" has length 4, a new key: start an empty list and add it.
"cat" has length 3: append it to that list.
"valve" has length 5, a new key: start an empty list and add it.
"gear" has length 4: append it to that list.

complexity.note: One pass with an O(1) average dictionary lookup and an append per word; the dictionary of lists holds every word once.
